1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

1	# Agent tools: info, examples, validate, render
2	
3	Four `@aura3d/cli` commands an agent runs inside a project so it can author, validate, render, inspect and correct without leaving the CLI. All four work offline: no network, no account, no Playwright. `render` needs a local Chrome (the same driver as `aura3d verify`).
4	
5	```bash
6	aura3d info                               # installed versions + engine namespaces and their members
7	aura3d info --name material.pbr           # one builder: signature and option keys (or close names for a guess)
8	aura3d examples "gold product on a pedestal"   # best recipe or template, with its source
9	aura3d examples --id recipe-11- --write src/main.ts
10	aura3d validate                           # static checks of src/ (or: aura3d validate src/main.ts)
11	aura3d render                             # build, serve, screenshot, diagnostics; --json for the report
12	aura3d render --no-build --json           # reuse dist/
13	aura3d render --url http://127.0.0.1:5173/ --out shot.png   # an already running dev server
14	aura3d verify --explain VALIDATE_SUBJECT_SMALL                  # cause and fix for any code below
15	```
16	
17	The loop: `examples` (start from working code) → edit → `validate` (seconds, no browser) → `render` (open the PNG it saves) → fix the first error code → repeat. `aura3d verify` remains the one-shot full pass (typecheck, assets, lint, build, render, inspect).

content.thinking:
I'm sketching out the solar system scale, setting orbit radii, sizes, and orbital periods for each planet relative to the sun to keep proportions reasonably realistic.

For animation speed I'm scaling angular velocity by period using a square-root ratio so inner planets visibly move faster while outer ones barely shift, which should still satisfy a "different speeds" check. For the camera, I'm planning a custom orbit controller handling pointer drag and wheel on the canvas, updating position each frame via setPose rather than relying on the engine's built-in controls.

For focusing on a planet, I'm blending the camera pose from its current state to a live target near the clicked planet over about 1.5 seconds with easing, capturing the starting pose at click time so interrupts (switching focus mid-transition) work smoothly, and reversing the same approach when unfocusing back to the overview.

For the offset direction, I need to avoid placing the camera on the planet's dark side relative to the star, so instead of a simple radial-outward position I'm blending tangent, inward-radial, and up vectors, and rotating that offset frame with the planet's orbital angle so it stays lit and consistent as the planet moves around the star.

I'm also working out camera distances based on planet size—roughly 4.5x size normally, 6x for ringed planets, and 6.5x specifically for Saturn to keep its rings in frame given a 45° vertical FOV—plus setting near/far clipping planes to 0.1 and 500 in the pose setup.

Now I'm figuring out picking logic: casting a ray from screen coordinates using the camera's forward/right/up vectors and FOV, then testing sphere intersections against each planet with a slightly padded radius plus a minimum angular tolerance (around 9px) so distant small planets are still clickable, picking whichever hit has the smallest t-value.

I also need to distinguish clicks from drags using pointer movement thresholds, make drags orbit the camera, and have wheel/drag ignored while focused. Then I want to verify my FOV assumption is correct by testing the pick function against a planet's known screen position computed from the engine's actual view-projection matrix, though I'm limited since I can only inspect via screenshots and console logs rather than direct interaction.

For the task state, I'll expose it as a frozen, read-only object on window with getters so planet positions compute live. Pausing should halt orbital motion and spin by freezing the simulation time accumulator while letting camera transitions continue in real time, and I'll add a DOM-based Pause/Play button positioned over the canvas.

I need to check index.html to see where the canvas is placed.

Since the canvas is at top-left and fixed size, I'm planning to position overlay panels and buttons as absolute elements anchored to the body at matching coordinates, rather than wrapping the canvas itself. I'm also sketching out a starfield background using tiny instanced spheres scattered far in the distance.

For lighting, I'm thinking a point light at the origin with high intensity to simulate the sun, plus a dim neutral environment so night sides aren't fully black, with a dark navy scene background instead of a space HDRI. For animation, I'm planning to use rotation and position setters on each node, with rings and moons as separate child nodes tracking their parent's position with their own tilt.

For planet surfaces, I'm generating canvas textures with seeded horizontal color bands and noise to mimic gas giant and rocky textures, feeding them into a PBR material with high roughness and white base color, falling back to flat colors if texture support is uncertain. For rings, I'm considering a canvas texture with radial stripes mapped so u follows radius and v follows angle, using blended alpha for gaps, applied to a double-sided annulus geometry since vertex color support is unclear. For orbit paths, I'm setting up looped line geometry with many points and testing emissive materials to get a glowing trail effect.

content.thinking:
I'm setting up the scene with a perspective camera and background, then wiring up a point light and a frame loop that updates node positions each tick using a clamped delta time.

For the planets I'm just applying a y-axis spin rotation rather than a full axis tilt, with the ring handled as a separate tilted node. Then I'm working out camera framing math — picking distance, elevation, and field-of-view values so the whole solar system fits in view at default zoom, checking horizontal and vertical extents against Neptune's orbit radius.

I'm clamping elevation between roughly 0.08 and 1.45 radians, and setting up a transition system that eases the camera smoothly between overview and focused poses over 1.5 seconds using linear interpolation on position and target, while checking that the straight-line path doesn't awkwardly clip through the sun.

For the focused pose, I'm computing the planet's position from its current orbital angle, then deriving the radial and tangential unit vectors so I can offset the camera relative to the planet's motion direction.

Camera offset combines a bit toward the star side with a backward-along-motion pull and slight height, so the lit hemisphere shows with the star glow in the background without needing the star itself in frame; the target locks to the planet's position. For Earth's moon, I'm setting its orbital radius relative to Earth's size, a smaller scale, and a fast rotation period so it reads clearly when Earth is focused.

I'll give Jupiter two moons and keep Mars without any, generalizing the moons array so each planet can have a different count cheaply. For the info panel, I want it to show the name, orbital period in Earth days, and distance from the star formatted with thousands separators, toggling visibility immediately on focus rather than waiting for a transition. Escape key and clicking empty space should both unfocus, and I'll skip ray-picking on rings and hover-cursor styling to keep things simple.

For the ready flag, I'll set `window.__EVAL_READY__` inside the first frame callback, deferring it one more animation frame to be sure the first draw has actually happened. I'm defining `__TASK_STATE__` on the window with a non-configurable property whose getter builds a fresh snapshot object each time, using nested getters for things like the planets array so that `JSON.stringify` still works correctly when the page evaluates it.

For world positions, planet meshes use the same simulation coordinates as my internal node data, and moons are excluded from the planets list. Stars use unlit emissive white spheres so bloom picks them up slightly at the 0.85 threshold.

I'm resolving the ambiguity around sphere "size" by checking the skeleton example — a size of 1.6 sitting at y=0.8 on the floor implies size is the diameter, so radius equals size divided by two, and I'll apply that convention consistently for the sun and planets.

Now I'm sizing each planet: assigning radii from Mercury through Neptune, giving the sun a radius of 3.5, and spacing orbital distances so Saturn's rings don't overlap Jupiter. I'm checking whether these distances still read well at the default camera distance and field of view, since smaller bodies like Mercury risk becoming only a few pixels wide — so I'm tightening the orbital spacing to keep everything visible and clickable.

I'm also setting up Earth's moon with its own orbit radius and size relative to Earth, and Jupiter's two moons at slightly larger distances, then planning a focus camera distance scaled to each planet's radius so zoomed-in views stay framed correctly. Now I'm starting to write the texture-generation function that paints procedural planet surfaces onto a canvas based on a base color and planet type.

Writing texture generation code...

Writing orbit geometry and material setup...

Now I'm adding pointer and wheel event handlers for drag-to-rotate and zoom-to-scroll camera controls, clamping distance and preventing default scroll behavior.

For hit testing, I'm computing ray-to-planet closest-approach distances in screen space, picking the nearest intersecting planet within a tolerance based on its radius and angular size, then handling the case where a click lands on empty space to deselect.

Clicking the already-focused planet does nothing. I'm positioning the info panel and return button absolutely within the canvas container, adding a small hint text at the bottom-left, and making sure pointer-events are set correctly so overlay elements don't block canvas interactions.

The planet and ring looks are procedural canvas textures, and the starfield is a ring of instanced points, so nothing is loaded from the network.

A panel shows its name, orbital period in Earth days, and distance in million km. Clicking empty space or pressing Escape eases back to the overview and hides the panel. In the overview you can drag to orbit and scroll to zoom within limits.
- **Pause:** The button reads "Pause" and switches to "Play". It stops all simulated motion, including spin and moons. Camera transitions still run while paused.

- **Orbital speeds:** Orbits are not to real scale. Each planet's orbital speed scales with the square root of its real period, so outer planets still visibly move.
